messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 57-year-old single man who works as a tutor, meeting students in library study rooms, at kitchen tables in their homes, and sometimes online when he can arrange it. When he speaks about the assault, he does so haltingly. He says he knows exactly what happened and at the same time cannot seem to put it into words. Certain parts are painfully sharp, almost overlit in his mind, while other parts feel missing, as if the sequence breaks apart when he gets too close to it. What remains especially clear is being alone with another man in a closed space, realizing he was no longer in control of what was happening, and the moment physical contact became something forced on him rather than chosen. That loss of autonomy is what still stands out most starkly to him. He remembers the feel of the man's hands with distressing clarity; then his account becomes fragmented, and he stops, saying he can see it but cannot say it.

In the weeks after the assault, David found that ordinary contact no longer felt ordinary. A hand on his shoulder, someone brushing past him in a crowded hallway, even the casual closeness of standing near another man could make his body tense before he had time to think. He had come to believe that his body was no longer something he could rely on. It reacted too fast, too strongly, and in ways that made him feel exposed. What frightened him most was that danger no longer seemed to announce itself clearly. He became certain that he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. In public he began watching other people closely, scanning faces, posture, tone, and distance for any sign that someone might harm him. Unfamiliar places felt particularly risky because he could not judge them quickly; if he did not know the exits, the layout, who might be around, or how close other people would be, he preferred not to go.

These habits began shaping his work. As a tutor, he started refusing new meeting locations unless he could picture them in advance. If a student suggested a different café or a new branch library, David often redirected them or offered online sessions instead. When he did meet in person, he always chose his seat based on how protected he felt, preferring a chair with a clear view of the room and an easy path out, never wanting to be cornered or surprised by someone approaching from behind. If a student's father or older brother was unexpectedly home and David found himself alone with another man in the house for even a brief moment, he became rigid and distracted, his attention pulled away from the lesson and toward monitoring the room.

Over time, he narrowed his life further to avoid emotional strain. He declined invitations, cut short conversations that felt too personal, and steered away from situations likely to stir strong feeling. He also avoided touch in an increasingly deliberate way. He kept more physical distance from others, stepped back from greetings, and arranged himself carefully so no one would brush against him. These choices made sense to him; avoiding contact and intense feeling seemed like the only way to get through the day without being overwhelmed. Smoking became woven into this routine. He would smoke before going into a tutoring session, after leaving one, and in the pauses between difficult moments, using the ritual to manage himself when he felt stirred up or on edge.

The cost has been a life that feels smaller and more solitary. David already lives alone, and he now experiences himself as fundamentally set apart from other people. Around others he often feels different in a way he cannot bridge, as though everyone else is participating in an ordinary social world whose rules no longer apply to him. He is especially aware of this when students or colleagues exchange easy gestures of familiarity that he cannot tolerate. He does not describe himself as simply shy or private; rather, he feels isolated by what happened and by how much effort it takes to stay watchful.

He sought help only recently, after noticing how much of his workday had become organized around safety calculations. He was spending as much energy deciding where to sit, who might be present, and how to avoid contact as he was actually tutoring. In session, he returns again and again to the same fear: that if he lets his guard down, if he is trapped, touched, or overpowered even briefly, he will have no way to protect himself. At the same time, what he hopes for is modest and deeply important to him. He wants to be able to do his job without constantly scanning the room, to enter a new place without immediately planning escape, and to feel that his own body is something he can inhabit rather than something that can betray him.
